content:
The Quran describes the natural world in many verses, and modern science has confirmed what they say. This article sets out four of the strongest cases, and shows what each verse says in its own words.

A word first about the Quran's own claim. The scholar Ismail al Faruqi argued that the "miracle" the Quran offers is its language: the challenge to produce a chapter like it (2:23) is addressed to the intellect of those who know Arabic, and it is a different kind of sign from the parting of a sea, which overwhelms the mind.[1] On that view the Quran's first proof is its language, and its accurate account of the natural world is a further sign beside it.

"Do you not see that God sends down water from the sky and leads it through the earth as springs?"[2] "God is who sends the winds that raise clouds, and spreads them in the sky as He wills, and you see the rain come out of them."[3] The verses speak of clouds, rain and groundwater, and they agree with what is known about each. Nothing in them has been overturned.

The Hebrew Bible says something similar (Ecclesiastes 1:7, where the rivers run to the sea and return to the place they came from), and Aristotle set out an account of evaporation and rainfall in his Meteorologica.[4] Those accounts mixed truth with error, and Aristotle's physics of the heavens has long been abandoned. The Quran's picture holds in every part, and it presents the cycle as a sign of God's provision.

The Quran describes human creation from a drop (nuṭfa), then a clinging thing (ʿalaqa), then a chewed lump (muḍgha), then bones clothed in flesh.[5] A standard textbook of embryology, in a later edition, reported close parallels with the stages it describes.[6]

Critics point to Galen, who had described stages, and to the order "bones, then flesh". The Quran's terms describe what the embryo looks like and does at each stage.

ʿAlaqa, "that which clings", fits the embryo implanted in the wall of the womb, and muḍgha, "a chewed lump", fits the embryo with its row of somites. The bones are then "clothed" with flesh, as the muscles form around the skeleton taking shape inside them.

The hadith add timings that complicate the picture. In a report in al-Bukhari the Prophet says that each person is gathered in the womb for forty days, then becomes an alaqa for a like period, then a mudgha for a like period, and then an angel is sent.[7] A report in Muslim speaks instead of the angel shaping the embryo after forty-two nights.[8]

The classical scholars reconciled the two in different ways, and the jurists used the timings in rulings on miscarriage and abortion. The classical scholars reconciled the reports with care, and their work shows the verses were read closely long before modern embryology.

"It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day. Each swims in an orbit."[9] The verse says that celestial bodies move on their own courses, which fits modern astronomy. A parallel verse, 21:33, says the same of the night, the day, the sun and the moon.

The word falak (orbit, sphere) served the astronomers of every age. Classical astronomers working within the Ptolemaic system took it as the track of each body, and the modern heliocentric system fits it just as well. The verse names the one thing that holds under every model: each body moves on its own appointed course, and nothing in the sky moves at random.

The classical scholars also show that the shape of the earth was never a problem for them. Ibn Hazm, in eleventh-century Spain, wrote that none of the leading Muslim scholars denied that the earth is a sphere, and cited the Quran's description of night wrapping around the day as support.[10]

Muslim astronomers measured the earth's circumference under the caliph al-Mamun. The scholars took the science of their day seriously and read the verses in harmony with it, which is the attitude this article recommends.

The same holds for Quran 51:47, which says, "We built the heaven with might, and We are expanding it," and which is cited for the expanding universe. The Arabic musiʿun can mean "expanding" and also "possessing vastness" or "able", and the classical commentators read it in the second sense.[11] The modern reading is carried by the word itself, and it sits beside the orbit verses as a second description of the heavens that science has confirmed.

"An ant said, 'O ants, enter your dwellings.'"[12] Ants do communicate by chemical signals and touch, and the story fits that.

The verse sits inside the story of Solomon, who had been taught the speech of the birds, and it records that he understood the ant and smiled. The marvel in the passage is therefore a gift given to one prophet, and the modern finding about pheromones is a side observation about the real animal behind it.

Anyone who has watched a column of ants part and re-form around an obstacle will recognise the picture without any laboratory. The verse is true to the animal, and it asks no more of the reader than attention to a small creature that most people step over.

The bottom line

The four cases point the same way. The water cycle, the orbits, the stages of the embryo and the speech of the ant are each described correctly, in words spoken in seventh-century Arabia, and nothing in them has been overturned by fourteen centuries of science.

The verses are best read in their own words, without stretching a word to fit the latest finding, and read that way they stand. The Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd had already advised that where demonstrated knowledge seems to conflict with the plain wording of a verse, the verse is to be read figuratively.[13] The Quran invites reflection on the creation, and it is best read for the questions it raises about the world.

Notes

  1. Ismail R. al Faruqi, Divine Transcendence and Its Expression (Kuala Lumpur: Muslim Youth Movement of Malaysia, 1983), III.D, on ijāz and the contrast with the miracles of earlier prophets.
  2. Quran 39:21.
  3. Quran 30:48.
  4. Ecclesiastes 1:7; Aristotle, Meteorologica, Book 1, on evaporation and rainfall.
  5. Quran 23:12–14; see also 96:2.
  6. The Developing Human, 3rd ed. (1982), the later edition with the Islamic additions.
  7. Sahih al-Bukhari 3208, Book of the Beginning of Creation, report of Abd Allah ibn Masud, checked on sunnah.com.
  8. Sahih Muslim 2645, Book of Destiny, report of Hudhayfa ibn Asid, checked on sunnah.com.
  9. Quran 36:40; see also 21:33.
  10. Ibn Hazm, al-Fisal fi al-milal wa-l-ahwa wa-l-nihal, on the sphericity of the earth, citing Quran 39:5.
  11. Quran 51:47; al-Tabari, commentary on 51:47.
  12. Quran 27:16–19.
  13. Ibn Rushd (Averroes), Fasl al-Maqal (The Decisive Treatise), on the interpretation of scripture when it appears to conflict with demonstrated knowledge.
